title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Introduction
content: Syncope and paroxysmal spells are non-epileptic, transient events that can mimic seizures but are not associated with the hypersynchronous, rhythmic discharges of cortical neurons that define epileptic seizures. [1] Syncope is defined as a transient loss of consciousness attributed to global cerebral hypoperfusion related to systemic vasodilation or decreased cardiac output. It is typically followed by rapid and complete recovery without a postictal period. Paroxysmal spells encompass a broader category of brief, transient events characterized by changes in consciousness and behavior. They may or may not be associated with a prodrome and full loss of consciousness. Paroxysmal spells can be caused by psychological disorders such as substance abuse and psychiatric disease or physiological events such as hypoglycemia, traumatic brain injury, and syncope. [2] [3] [4] Importantly, both syncope and paroxysmal spells are clinically different from epileptic seizures and involve separate underlying pathophysiologies. Critically, sycope and seizure are not associated with the epileptiform cortical discharges on EEG that are characteristic of epileptic seizures.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Introduction -- Syncope
content: As most paroxysmal events are syncopal, the remainder of this discussion will focus primarily on syncope. Physiologically, syncope is a transient loss of consciousness as a result of cerebral hypoperfusion. As such, syncope varies from other etiologies of loss of consciousness in that it does not include head trauma or a post-ictal state. Syncope, instead, results in the complete and rapid resolution of mental status. It may have myoclonic jerking, but no persistent generalized tonic-clonic movement. Rather than a disease, syncope is a symptom of an underlying pathology ranging from benign to life-threatening. Patients are often divided into "low-risk" and "high-risk" groups. Features of high-risk syncope include syncope associated with exertion, chest pain or palpitations, evidence of cardiac arrhythmia or structural defects, and new or previously unknown EKG abnormalities. [5] The etiology, epidemiology, evaluation, treatment, and management of these patients vary greatly. In the United States, hospitalization costs for syncope are estimated to be $5300 per admission and more than $2 billion annually, outpacing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma combined. As extensive workups can be costly, time-consuming, and often unnecessary, a growing cadre of management tools has been created to aid in the evaluation of patients with syncope. These tools are designed to categorize patients into risk categories and identify and treat patients with dangerous or high-risk syncope. [6] [7]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Introduction -- Psychological Conditions
content: Data suggest that men with psychiatric disease may have an increased incidence of syncope or paroxysmal events of unknown etiology. This data should lead clinicians to consider screening for psychiatric disorders in patients presenting with transient loss of consciousness when a clear etiology is not identified after a thorough medical workup.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Introduction -- Psychological Conditions
content: Among patients with a history of substance use disorder, 45% have been found to have unexplained syncope. This suggests that prior and current substance use is also associated with increased incidence of transient loss of consciousness of unknown etiology. Patients evaluated in the emergency department or even hospitalized with syncope of unknown etiology may benefit from toxicology screening and possible detoxification referral.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Introduction -- Hypoglycemia
content: Hypoglycemia can cause a transient loss of consciousness, but generally is not regarded as a cause of syncope because, rather than recovering spontaneously, it requires glucose for recovery. Hypoglycemia is defined as low blood sugar levels accompanied by associated symptoms. In patients without diabetes mellitus, this is usually manifested at glucose levels below 50 mg/dl. In patients with diabetes or chronically elevated blood glucose levels, symptoms may manifest at other levels; specifically, people with chronically elevated blood glucose levels may experience hypoglycemic symptoms at blood glucose levels typically defined as normal. To diagnose hypoglycemia, symptoms and blood sugar levels must improve with the administration of exogenous glucose. Hypoglycemia can affect the central nervous system, leading to lightheadedness, nausea, flashes of light, focal neurological deficits, transient loss of consciousness, and seizure. It is, therefore, paramount that patients with any paroxysmal spell or loss of consciousness receive a fingerstick glucose test.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Introduction -- Traumatic Brain Injury
content: Traumatic brain injury is an intracranial impairment, often due to external forces. These forces may include blunt or penetrating trauma to the head, causing acceleration/deceleration injury to the cerebral cortex. Intracerebral bleeding, lacerations, and diffuse axonal injuries may result. Injuries, such as an epidural hematoma, may cause a brief state of loss of consciousness, with rapid return of, usually altered consciousness. Other injuries, such as a large subdural hematoma or diffuse axonal injury, may cause worsening mentation and coma over hours to days. This is a result of increased intracranial pressure, leading to decreased cerebral perfusion pressure and finally, neuronal ischemia. Diagnosis is by clinical history and CT imaging, although MRI may be more specific for secondary trauma. Management is to reduce intracranial pressure and edema.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Etiology
content: The etiology of syncope varies greatly, and the causes range from benign to immediately life-threatening. Examples of benign causes include dehydration and vasovagal syncope, also known as neurocardiogenic syncope. Vasovagal syncope is the predominant cause of syncope worldwide, particularly in young patients. Concerning or high-risk causes of syncope include cardiac arrhythmia (eg, ventricular tachycardia, bradyarrhythmias), conduction system disease (eg, sick sinus syndrome, high-grade atrioventricular block), structural heart disease (eg, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as Brugada syndrome, Long QT syndrome, and arrythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia. Other serious causes include acute blood loss leading to anemia and pulmonary embolism. All of these conditions involve transient hypoperfusion to the brain and require prompt evaluation in the emergency department. [8] [9]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Epidemiology
content: The prevalence of syncope is approximately 20% in the general population. The risk of recurrence is approximately 13.5%. Females have a greater prevalence than men. In retrospective studies, the etiology of syncope is undetermined in 37% of cases. Most cases of syncope, especially in young patients, are reflex-mediated neurocardiogenic and benign. [10]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathophysiology of syncope varies by its etiology. In benign syncope, such as vasovagal syncope, the vagus nerve is often overstimulated, thus causing a transient loss of consciousness. The most common causes are due to emotional distress or excitement, pain,  temperature intolerance, cough, laughter, micturition, or defecation. All etiologies require a careful history, physical examination, and evaluation, particularly when concerned for cardiac or blood loss-related triggers,  as syncope may be a predictor of a dangerous, life-threatening pathology.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: A thorough and focused history, along with a physical exam, are the most important aspects of the initial workup for syncope. In fact, healthcare costs and diagnostic time can be substantially reduced when clinicians obtain a comprehensive history. [11] Multiple decision support tools have been developed and validated to aid in the risk stratification of patients presenting with syncope. Such tools include the Boston Syncope pathway, the San Francisco Syncope tool, and the Canadian Syncope Risk Score. Importantly, these tools have been validated in identifying patients who are likely to have low-risk syncope and may be appropriate for discharge. It is always important to consider the patient's history before applying a clinical decision tool to ensure they are within the validated population.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- History and Physical
content: The history of a patient presenting with syncope should assess for the presence of prodromal symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, vision changes, diaphoresis, nausea, or palpitations. The presence or absence of these symptoms helps distinguish vasovagal syncope from other, more severe types of syncope. Furthermore, obtaining a tailored personal and family history of cardiac disease and cardiac death is critical. Medications often contribute to syncopal events and need to be verified. A physical examination should include auscultation for a murmur, as well as orthostatic vital signs.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: In the United States, evaluation and treatment guidelines for syncope are primarily based on the 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Syncope, published by the American College of Cardiology (ACC), the American Heart Association (AHA), and the Heart Rhythm Society (HRS). Generally, the valuation of syncope should focus on risk stratification between low-, intermediate-, and high-risk cases. As noted, a thorough history, including medication review and physical exam, will aid in risk stratification. New medications, such as beta blockers, nitrates, diuretics, and antiarrhythmics, should be carefully considered as potential contributors. A family history of sudden cardiac death is a significant predictor of adverse outcomes. [12] [13] [14]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Benign or low-risk characteristics include being younger than 40, experiencing syncope after standing from a sitting position, and having prodromal symptoms such as warmth, nausea, cough, or micturition before syncope. Situational or emotional triggers, such as pain or emotional distress, also suggest a benign cause. In children, psychogenic pseudosyncope may present similarly and should be considered when appropriate. Volume depletion or dehydration is a common cause of syncope in young patients, and orthostatic evaluation can be considered as part of the workup. Rarely, a cerebrovascular accident, such as an intracranial bleed, can cause reflex-mediated syncope; however, this is uncommon in the absence of focal neurologic findings.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Features that indicate a high-risk event include exertional syncope, concomitant chest pain, history of congestive heart failure, aortic stenosis, left ventricular outflow tract disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, prior coronary artery disease, congenital heart disease, and pacemaker or cardioverter-defibrillator placement. Recurrent syncope with multiple episodes in 6 months should warrant further evaluation, regardless of age. [15]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Vital sign abnormalities, such as hypotension, may indicate hypovolemia or an acute bleed. A focused physical examination evaluating for pallor or evidence of bleeding should always be included. Consider sources of bleeding, such as gastrointestinal bleeding and menorrhagia, as these may not be immediately apparent on exam. Obtain labs to evaluate hemoglobin and hematocrit in patients where hypovolemia or anemia is suspected. Other vital sign abnormalities, such as bradycardia, may indicate arteriovenous (AV) dissociation. Hypoxia can indicate a pulmonary embolism. Physical exam findings of a new murmur can indicate dangerous valvular pathologies, such as aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: All patients should receive a screening electrocardiogram (ECG). ECG features, such as a new left bundle branch block, Brugada pattern, arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia, prolonged QTc, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy patterns, suggest high risk and indicate a need for further workup. Similarly, sinus bradycardia, dysrhythmias, and second or third-degree AV blocks should all warrant further workup.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Evaluation
content: Please note that all testing outside of ECG should be considered on a case-by-case basis. Advanced imaging of the head, such as CT or MRI, is not found to be diagnostically helpful in cases of uncomplicated syncope and should be reserved for cases presenting with evidence of head trauma or focal neurologic deficit.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with low-risk syncope, as determined by a comprehensive evaluation including history, physical examination, and screening ECG, can be safely discharged home. Without any high-risk features, the likely cause of the syncope is benign; vasovagal and dehydration are the most common. Orthostasis in young patients often differentiates between vasovagal and dehydration. Patients can be rehydrated and discharged if symptoms resolve. If the young patient has recurrent syncope without high-risk features, a non-emergent echocardiogram can be scheduled for the patient as an outpatient. Long-term management may include the use of a beta-blocker, compression stockings, or fludrocortisone. [16] [17] [18] [19]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with high-risk syncope require further observation or workup. Specifically, studies have been conducted to investigate the utility of observation units in the emergency department for patients with syncope as a means to reduce healthcare expenditures. These studies have shown similar outcomes, adverse events, and a reduction in costs when compared to inpatient hospitalizations.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Testing done in observation units or as an inpatient should be tailored to the patient’s syncopal evaluation and etiology. If there are signs and symptoms of acute coronary syndrome, such as chest pain or ECG ischemic changes, serial troponins should be done. Exercise stress testing may also be helpful.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with a worrisome cardiac history, such as significant coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, are at high risk for structural abnormalities and arrhythmia. These patients should have an echocardiogram to evaluate for worsening structural abnormalities that would decrease left ventricular outflow. The treatment may include an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). Patients with a history of ventricular dysrhythmias are at high risk for recurrence. The recurrence of syncope within 6 months may also indicate a dysrhythmia. Patients with an ICD or pacemaker already in place should have their device interrogated to determine if a dysrhythmia occurred.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: All patients with worrisome cardiac histories should have 24-hour telemetry observation and evaluation for ICD placement. Patients with conduction disease on ECG, a new murmur on physical exam, or a concerning family history of sudden cardiac death should be evaluated for structural and valvular disorders with an echocardiogram, telemetry, and home telemetry. Often, these patients may require a pacemaker or ICD.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Treatment / Management
content: All patients with suspected anemia as the cause of hypovolemia should have a complete blood count (CBC), type and screen, and evaluation for the etiology of the bleed. Patients with concern for an acute intracranial bleed as the cause of syncope should have a CT of their head and likely neurosurgical consultation. Finally, patients with hypoxia, unexplained tachycardia, or signs of DVT should undergo a workup for venous thromboembolism and pulmonary emboli.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Prognosis
content: In cases of low-risk syncope, prognosis is typically excellent, particularly in young patients presenting with vasovagal related syncope. [20] These patients oftne recover spontaneously and may require no ongoing management. Patients with high risk features of syncope, however, have poorer outcomes. This often relates to having underlying cardiac disease of some type and require ongoing medical care and management.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Complications
content: Complications from syncope arise in two main categories: physical injury due to syncopal episode and adverse outcomes related to misdiagnosis. When an individal loses conciousness and falls, they are at risk for serious physical injury including head trauma, cervical spinal injury, facial fractures and blunt force injuries to the torso and extremities. This must always be considered when a patient reports loss of conciousness and associated fall. Patients taking blood thinner medications such as anti-coagulation or anti-platelet medications, patients with evidence of ongoing altered mental status or focal neurologic deficit should have these symptoms evaluated in parallel while also investigating the syncopal event. Causes of such presentations include intracranial bleeding or spinal cord injury. [21] On the other hand, complications also arise when high risk syncope is miscategorized as low risk. The risk of adverse events - such as sudden cardiac death, recurrent syncope, and prolonged hospitalization - increases significantly when a patient is miscategorized. This underscores the critical importance of obtaining a thorough history, physical examination and electrocardiogram on all patients presenting with syncope.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Consultations
content: Consultation for patients presenting with syncope depends on the suspected etiology and associated injuries. In patients presenting with low-risk syncope and no evidence of traumatic injury, consultation may not be required and outpatient follow up is sufficient.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Consultations
content: However, if a patient has sustained an inury, appropriate specialty service consultation should be performed. Examples include orthopaedic surgery for fractures, neurologic surgery for intracranial bleeding or spinal trauma, and reconstructive facial surgery services for facial fractures. Neurology consultation may be indicated if the syncope is suspected to be related to a primary neurological cause such as a seizure or concern for an alternate neurology primary cause of the syncopal episode such as transient ischemic attack. Toxicology should be consulted in cases of syncope related to ingestion such as alcohol, recreational drugs and prescrption drugs. Cardiology should be consulted when ever an episode of syncope is suspected to be related to a cardic cause.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: In many cases, episdoes of transient loss of consiousness are due to bengin causes especially in young and otherwise healthy people. Experiencing syncope, or passing out, can often be scary and a cause of concern for patients. It is important to discuss an episode of loss of conciousness with your doctor to determine next steps and necessary medical testing. In patients with known cardiac conditions, syncope can be more concerning and should prompt urgent medical evaluation. Be sure to note symptoms associated with a loss of conciousness and when they occur. Examples include chest pain, shortness of breath or dizziness just prior to losing conciousness. Additionally, patients should take note of the activity they were doing when the event occured such as excercising, using the bathroom or resting. Providing these details to their doctor can help them determine not only the cause of their loss of conciousness, but also help identify any high risk features of the event. This guides medical evaluation and follow up care.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Syncope and paroxysmal spells cover a huge range of conditions ranging from benign to life threatening. All patients presenting for evaluation of syncope require history taking (focused on prodromal symptoms and features of the event, family and medication history), physical examination and electrocardiogram. Patients with evidence of traumatic injury associated with the syncopal episode also require evaluation of their injuries. Appropriate risk stratification of patients into low-, intermediate- and high- risk categories helps in determining depth of medical workup, disposition and follow up care. Patients presenting with low risk syncope can often be discharged home with outpatient follow up. High risk patients may require inpatient hospitalization for ongoing evaluation including echocardiogram and cardiology procedures such as implantable pacemaker device insertion.

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: There are many causes of syncope, and thus, the condition is best managed by an interprofessional team that includes an emergency department physician, primary care physician, nurse practitioner, cardiologist, neurologist, pharmacist, and specialty trained nurses. [22]

title: Syncope and Related Paroxysmal Spells(Archived) -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Emergency department and primary care physicians are often tasked with evaluating patients presenting with syncope for the first time and may have unknown high-risk features of their presentation. They are responsible for performing an initial evaluation and determining if a patient requires specialty evaluation as part of their medical care. This may include surgical subspecialty evaluation for injuries sustained in a fall related to syncope as well as cardiology consultation in cases of syncope of cardiac origin.
